Kāpālika
(‘one who uses a कपाल [or skull as a cup]’)
------------------------------------------
See ŚAIVISM.

kapālabhāti
------------------------------------------
Texts on हठयोग prescribe various methods for the internal purification of the body that help in maintaining it in good health. The षट्कर्मस् or six practices are an important prescription given by them.
The कपालभाति (vide Gheranḍa Saṁhitā 1.56-59) is the last of these six practices. It is, again, of three kinds:
vātakrama—Also called ‘vāma-krama’ it consists in drawing air through the left nostril and expelling it through the right and then, reversing the process.
vyutkrama—In this, the योगि draws water through both the nostrils and expels it through the mouth slowly.
śītkrama—This is the reverse of the above-mentioned practice, viz., drawing water through the mouth and then expelling through the nostrils.
See also ṢAṬKARMAS.

kapāla
(‘that which protects the head’)
------------------------------------------
Kapāla is skull. Some of the fierce deities of the Hindu pantheon like Kaṅkāla भैरव, Bhikṣāṭanamūrti (both being the terrible aspects of शिव) as also Kālī are shown carrying skull-cups or skull-pots, either for receiving alms or for drinking the blood of their victims.
The story connected with the Bhikṣāṭanamūrti aspect of शिव narrates how शिव nipped the fifth head of the arrogant ब्रह्मा and how it (the skull) stuck to his finger. Because of this sin, he had to roam about the earth as a mendicant for expiating that sin, finally getting rid of that skull (head) at काशी or वाराणसी.
Vampires and cemetery spirits (Vetālas) are believed to carry the skulls of their victims and drink their blood in them.
The sect of the Kāpālikas has made the कपाल, a part of its paraphernalia. Burnt pot-sherds used for baking puroḍāśas (rice-cakes) are also called ‘kapālas’.

Kapisthala-Kāṭhaka-Saṁhitā
------------------------------------------
This is a Saṁhitā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda group. The only manuscript available is incomplete. Its स्वर system (Vedic intonation) resembles that of the Ṛgveda.
It has 64 chapters spread over 8 aṣṭakas. The following are the details as available now:
First अष्टक: It is complete with eight chapters.
Second अष्टक: Damaged and incomplete
Third अष्टक: Chapters 9 to 24 have been lost.
Forth अष्टक: Chapters 25 to 31 are intact. Chapter 32 is lost. Chapter 27 is the famous Rudrādhyāya.
Fifth अष्टक: All chapters except the 33rd, have been recovered.
Sixth अष्टक: The 43rd Chapter has been lost. The rest—seven chapters—are available.

The contents are similar to the other Saṁhitās of this Veda.

Kapila
------------------------------------------
He was a celebrated sage, considered as the fifth इन्चर्नतिओन् of Lord विष्णु (Bhāgavata 1.3; 3.24). He was the brother of अरुन्धती (wife of the sage वसिष्ठ) and the only son of कर्दम and देवहूति.
He taught spiritual wisdom to his मोथेर् देवहूति. This part of the Bhāgavata is known as the Kapilagītā (3.25-33). This teaching contains not only the Sāṅkhya philosophy but also अष्टाङ्ग-योग and भक्तियोग.
The Sāṅkhyadarśana (the Sāṅkhya-sūtras) is attributed to him.
The sixty-thousand sons of the king सगर were reduced to ashes when they tried to attack him thinking that he was the person who had stolen the horse of the अश्वमेध sacrifice of their ड़थेर्.
He was against the sacrifice of a cow in the Vedic याग called Gosava as per the incident quoted in the Mahābhārata (Śāntiparva 273).
The Bhagavadgītā extols his greatness that कृष्ण is कपिल among the सिद्धस् or perfected sages (10.26).
